overview: This record covers modern Bulgaria from the state established in 1878 through monarchy, communist government and parliamentary democracy. It is distinct from the medieval Bulgar labels. Buildings, scientific work and living community traditions show how political change intersected with education, food and daily life.

periods.title: Principality and kingdom
periods.summary: Modern statehood was restored in 1878; full independence was declared in 1908. The monarchy ended in 1946.

periods.title: Communist government
periods.summary: A people's republic brought nationalization and forced agricultural collectivization; one-party rule shaped public life.

periods.title: Democratic transition and republic
periods.summary: The transition began in 1989, followed by a new constitution in 1991 and European Union membership in 2007.

items.text: The Tarnovo Constitution of 1879 set the framework for Bulgaria's early parliamentary institutions. Its operation was interrupted during authoritarian periods, so the existence of a constitution did not mean uninterrupted democratic government.

The National Assembly building, designed by Constantin Jovanovic and constructed in 1884-1886, made the new institutions physically visible in Sofia. Its neo-Renaissance design belongs to a wider European architectural conversation.

Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia united in 1885; Ferdinand declared independence in 1908. These were separate steps, which is why the map's 1878 beginning should not be read as the date when every question of sovereignty was settled.

In March 1943, Bulgarian authorities deported more than 11,000 Jews from occupied Macedonia, Thrace and Pirot into German custody; almost all were murdered at Treblinka. This responsibility is part of the country's wartime history.

Public and political protests helped stop deportations from Bulgaria's core provinces, but Jews there still endured discriminatory laws, forced labour, dispossession and internal expulsion. Survival and persecution must both be remembered.

After the Second World War, the communist government nationalized businesses and forced farmland into cooperatives. Changes of ownership and work reached into family routines, rather than remaining only a story about leaders.

Chitalishta are community cultural centres, first established in 1856, before modern statehood. Communities created places for learning and cultural activities; older members continue to pass knowledge and skills to younger participants.

These centres organize performances, celebrations, exhibitions and local documentation. Their collaboration with schools joins formal lessons with skills learned by doing. Learning continues outside the classroom through community activities.

For the beginning of March, people exchange and wear red-and-white thread ornaments associated with wishes for a safe spring. The tradition is shared across several neighbouring countries, not exclusively Bulgarian.

A first blossom, swallow or stork can signal that it is time to remove the thread. Families, teachers and craftworkers pass on the making skills. Nature gets a say in the calendar: the stork does not need a smartphone reminder.
Stamen Grigorov investigated the microbes in Bulgarian yogurt in 1905. The achievement was explaining fermentation already practiced by food makers, not inventing yogurt from nothing.

The Serdica dairy in Sofia introduced mechanized pasteurization for industrial yogurt production in 1960. The producer's history describes earlier cauldrons, starter cultures and reusable containers, connecting laboratory knowledge with the practical work of feeding people.

Sofia's Central Mineral Baths were built in 1906-1913, with colourful majolica decoration. Their architects treated a place for washing as an important civic building. The former bath now houses the regional history museum: the building itself is one of its historical objects.

България е република с парламентарно управление. This means “Bulgaria is a republic with a parliamentary form of government.” It is Article 1(1) of the 1991 Constitution, written in modern Bulgarian using Cyrillic, not a medieval inscription.

ending.text: Bulgaria continues as a sovereign parliamentary republic. The monarchy's end in 1946 and the transition from communist rule beginning in 1989 were changes of government, not the disappearance of the country. It joined the European Union in 2007.

sources.title: Bulgarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs: History
sources.note: Medieval and modern chronology: Christianity under Boris, Byzantine conquest 1018, renewed Bulgarian rule 1180s, Ottoman conquest, 1878 restoration, 1885 union, 1908 independence, 1946 republic and 1989 transition. Avoid its inaccurate compressed alphabet chronology and disputed massacre totals.

sources.title: US Holocaust Memorial Museum: Bulgaria
sources.note: Persecution of Jews: anti-Jewish measures, deportations from occupied Macedonia, Thrace and Pirot in March 1943; protests and cancellation in core Bulgarian provinces did not end internal displacement or forced labor.
